subject: Cloud Computing
title: CQRS: Reads vs. Writes
description: A micro-lesson that makes CQRS: Reads vs. Writes usable.

hook.text: Your app reads data 100x more than it writes. Why use the same model for both? CQRS says: don't.

buildup.text: Command Query Responsibility Segregation uses separate models for reading and writing data.

discovery.text: The write side handles commands and business logic. The read side serves optimized, denormalized views.

twist.text: CQRS adds complexity. Eventually consistent reads mean the read side might be briefly out of date after a write.

climax.text: For high-read, low-write systems, CQRS delivers massive performance gains. For simple apps, it's overkill.

punchline.text: Separate reads from writes. Each can be optimized independently.

quiz.question: What is the core idea behind CQRS?
options: Using separate optimized models for reading and writing data
Running all database queries in a single thread
Storing data only in memory, never on disk

details.summary: CQRS separates the read model from the write model in an application. Commands that change state go through one path, while queries that read state use a different, optimized path. This allows each side to scale and evolve independently.
details.whyItMatters: Most applications read far more than they write. CQRS lets you optimize each path separately, improving performance and simplifying complex domain logic.
takeaways: Read and write operations use separate optimized models
Each side can scale independently based on load patterns
Often paired with event sourcing for full auditability

faq.question: When should you use CQRS?
faq.answer: CQRS is valuable when read and write loads differ significantly, when the read model needs denormalized data for performance, or when the domain logic for writes is complex. Simple CRUD applications rarely benefit from the added complexity.

faq.question: Does CQRS mean eventual consistency?
faq.answer: Not necessarily, but it often does. If the read model is updated asynchronously from writes, there is a delay. Some implementations use synchronous updates for strong consistency at the cost of tighter coupling between the two sides.
